title: Three ways to fail at giving feedback
author: Luca
summary: Drawing on his own management failures, the author walks through three distinct feedback approaches he personally tried and abandoned, each illustrated with a realistic dialogue and traced through short-, mid-, and long-term consequences. 'Brutal honesty' felt virtuous in the moment but produced an escalating cycle of anger and eventually a report who stopped bringing problems forward at all; the HR-recommended 'sandwich method' delivered two compliments around a piece of criticism so gently that the actual feedback disappeared entirely, leaving the manager expecting change that never came; and the 'therapy session' approach of purely empathetic listening ended up unpacking feelings so thoroughly that the manager found himself defending his own request rather than holding a standard, ultimately teaching the underperforming employee that low performance was acceptable. The piece's explicit diagnosis of why all three fail is structural: brutal honesty skips the shared reality needed to receive tough feedback, the sandwich buries the message between instructions to disregard it, and the therapy session substitutes unpacking the past for addressing the future — setting up a promised follow-up post about what actually works.
points: 'Brutal honesty' is illustrated with a specific failed exchange and its long-term cost named explicitly: 'communication breaks down completely and he stops bringing you problems.'

The HR-trained 'sandwich method' (compliment, criticism, compliment) is shown to fail at the point of delivery itself — the recipient hears two compliments and a vague suggestion, and changes nothing.

The 'therapy session' approach, built around deep empathetic listening, is shown paradoxically ending with the manager defending his own request rather than holding a standard, teaching the employee that low performance is accepted.

All three approaches are diagnosed with a common root failure: they either skip shared reality, bury the message, or substitute the past for the future — none actually deliver an actionable, received message.

The piece is structured as the first of a two-part series, explicitly withholding the 'actually works' solution for a follow-up post, and grounded entirely in the author's own real managerial mistakes rather than abstract theory.
quotes: I started managing people at 27 and believed that saying things straight was the honest thing to do... In practice, I was calling myself virtuous while being an asshole.
long-term: communication breaks down completely and he stops bringing you problems; if you find out about them, you are forced to react urgently and have limited options.

You take a fluffy piece of white bread (i.e. a compliment), put some shit on top of it (i.e. the actual feedback) and then close it with another piece of white bread (i.e. another compliment) - hence its street name.
short-term: you are happy he took it well, but he hears two compliments and a suggestion and changes nothing
the therapy session ends up unpacking the past and disregarding the future, while you justify to your report why you are delivering the feedback in the first place.
None of these methods work: brutal honesty fails to create the safe environment and shared reality that are foundational to receiving a tough message.
